text: Go outside your classroom. Stand still for two minutes.
Look for grass in a crack, insects near a wall, or birds overhead. Choose two plants. Compare their leaves. What differences can you describe?
A planted tree and a plant growing without anyone sowing it both belong in your record. You do not need to know how something arrived before you can observe it.
This chapter is about that variety. How much of it is there? How do we make sense of it? And why are the living things in one place so different from the living things in another?
2.1 The Variety Around Us
A quick glance may tell you that a tree is there. A closer look can reveal the shape of its leaves, where its branches begin, or insects on its bark. Listening may reveal a bird you cannot see.
Looking carefully is a skill. Like any skill, it gets better with practice.
Practise looking closely in the investigation below. Tables 2.1 and 2.2 show possible records; your own entries may be different.

Investigate
**You will need:** a notebook, a pencil, a water bottle.
**What to do:**
1. Before the visit, copy the headings of Tables 2.1 and 2.2 into your notebook. Leave room for your own rows.
2. With your teacher, spend one period in a garden, park or school ground. Record the place, date and time.
3. Walk slowly, then stop at a safe place. Stand still and listen for thirty seconds. What different sounds can you hear?
4. Add a row for each kind of plant or animal you observe. If you do not know its name, describe or sketch it. For example: "small plant, three leaves together, near the tap".
5. Record only what you can establish. Write "not seen" for a feature you looked for but did not see. Do not pluck leaves or flowers or disturb animals.
Compare your records with a partner. Which living things were difficult to find or describe? What made them difficult?
**Safety:** Stay with your group. Do not touch any animal. Do not put your fingers into holes or under stones.
In these two example tables, a dash means that a feature was not recorded. It does not mean the feature is absent. A plant without flowers today may flower in another season.

Table 2.1: Example plant records
Name / description | Stem | Leaves | Flowers | Anything else
Common grass | Soft and thin | One thin leaf at a time | — | Grows in a thick patch
Tulsi | Hard and thin | Leaves in pairs, facing each other | Small, pinkish purple | Smells strong when rubbed
Hibiscus | Hard and woody | Broad leaves with toothed edges | Red flower |
Grass                         Tulsi                         Hibiscus
Read across a row to connect a plant with its features. Then read down a column to compare that feature across plants. Which differences would be hardest to show in a drawing?
The pictures show the three plants named in Table 2.1. They are enlarged by different amounts so you can see their features; do not use their printed heights to compare their actual sizes.
Were any two plants in your record alike in every feature you recorded? Would that prove they were the same kind of plant? What else could you examine?

Table 2.2: Example animal records
Name / description | Where you saw it | Doing / eating | How it moved | Anything else
Crow | On a wall, then a tree | Pecking at something | Walks, then flies | Carried a twig away
Ant | Along the edge of a step | Carrying a crumb | Walks | Six legs; followed the ant in front
A moving animal may disappear before you finish recording it. Try watching from one place as well as walking slowly. Which method helped you find which animals?

Separate what you saw from what you infer. The crow was seen on a wall and in a tree; that does not tell us every place it lives. "Pecking at something" does not identify its food. What further observation could help?
The variety of living things found in one region is called its **biodiversity**.
Your school ground has its own biodiversity. So does a pond. So does a forest, a seashore, and even the soil in a flowerpot.
Your search lasted one period. Name two kinds of living things that your method might have missed. Plan one change to the time, place or method that could help you find them.
Living Things Need Each Other
The living things in a place are not just sharing space. They are joined to each other.

A tree can provide shade for smaller plants and nesting places for birds. Some birds feed on insects on its bark. A fruit-eating bird may carry a seed away; the seed can grow if it reaches suitable conditions. Fallen leaves provide food for decomposers, which help return nutrients to the soil.
Removing a tree can remove shade, nest sites and a source of fallen leaves. The effects depend on which organisms use it and what other resources are available nearby.

Choose one plant or animal from your own record. Draw it in the centre of a notebook page. Add other living things it may depend on, or that may depend on it. Use arrows labelled "food", "shelter" or another relationship. Mark each link as observed, read about, or still a guess. Compare your diagram with a partner. Choose one uncertain link and suggest how you could check it. If one organism disappeared from your diagram, which links would be affected? Could another organism supply the same resource? Explain what you know and what you would need to find out.
2.2 Making Sense of the Variety
Your records may contain many kinds of living things. Grouping them can help you compare a feature without searching through every entry.
In a stationery shop, keeping pens together helps a customer find a pen. Arranging goods by price answers a different question: what can I buy with this amount of money?
Scientists do the same with living things. Putting things into groups by the features they share is called **grouping**.

Investigate
**You will need:** old magazines or newspapers, scissors, glue, small cards.
**What to do:**
1. Cut out pictures of plants and animals. Paste one on each card. Try to make at least thirty cards in the class.
2. Work in groups of five or six. Put all your cards together.
3. Sort the pile into groups. You decide what the groups will be.
4. Write down, in one line, the rule you used.
5. Now mix all the cards again. Sort them a second time, using a completely different rule.
Compare both your sortings with another group's.
Did any two groups in the class use the same rule?
**Safety:** Use scissors carefully, with your teacher’s guidance.
A Grouping Needs a Clear Rule
Take one sorted group and check every card against its rule. Two different rules can both be useful, but a card can still be placed incorrectly.
Different groups may use size, food or surroundings. Check what the pictures actually show before using these features.
Some ways of grouping

Choose a rule to suit your question, then apply it consistently. If a picture does not show the feature you need, mark it "not enough information". A picture without a visible flower does not prove that the plant never flowers.
A gardener comparing shade might group plants by height. Someone studying their flowers would need a different grouping. Explain what your rule helps you find out and what it leaves out.
Scientists also study groups whose members share several inherited features. Knowing one feature can then help us predict others. Later in this chapter, you will test such a connection.
How would a library arranged by book size help a reader? What would be harder to find?
2.2.1 Grouping Plants
Look at Table 2.1 again. The features you wrote there — stem, leaves, flowers — are the same features we can use to sort plants.
Begin with stems: their firmness, whether they are woody, and where they branch. Examine plants your teacher says are safe to handle.

Investigate
**What to do:**
1. Go out to the same place as before. Choose six plants of clearly different sizes.
2. Stand next to each one. Is it shorter than you, about your height, or taller?
3. Look at the stem near the ground. Is it green or brown?
4. Bend the stem very gently with one finger. Does it bend, or is it stiff? **Stop as soon as you feel it resist. A broken stem can kill the plant.**
5. See where the branches start. Near the ground, or higher up?
6. Record these features using the headings in Table 2.3. Group your plants by shared stem features and explain your rule.
Did height and stem features give you the same groups? Which plants were difficult to place?

Table 2.3: Grouping plants by height and stem
Plant | Height compared with you | Stem colour | Stem texture | Branching
Mango | Taller | Brown | Hard | High
Rose | About the same | Brown | Hard | Low
Tomato | Shorter | Green | Soft | Low
Herbs, Shrubs and Trees
Compare your records with the descriptions below. Your sample may not contain all three forms, and young or pruned plants may be harder to classify.
Plants with soft, non-woody stems are called **herbs**. Many are small, such as mint, coriander and tomato, but height alone does not define a herb.
**Shrubs** are woody plants that usually branch close to the ground, often with several main stems. A rose bush is an example. Observe the branching as well as the height.
**Trees** are woody plants that usually develop a main trunk supporting a crown of branches. Mango is an example. A young mango is still a tree even when it is shorter than a mature tomato plant.
Woody stems support branches and can thicken as a plant grows. Look at the base of a tree and then a herb: what differences can you describe without damaging either?
Mango · tree                 Rose · shrub                 Tomato · herb
A banana plant is a large herb. Its trunk-like structure is a **pseudostem**, made from tightly overlapping leaf bases rather than a woody trunk. Its height does not make it a tree.
Plants That Cannot Stand Up
Not every plant can hold itself up.

Some plants have stems that are too weak to stand. So they climb up something else — a wall, a fence, a stick, or another plant. These are called **climbers**. A money plant is a climber. So is a grape vine.
Other plants also have weak stems. But instead of climbing, they spread flat along the ground. These are called **creepers**. Pumpkin and watermelon plants are creepers.

Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, not a separate woody/non-woody division. A grape vine is a woody climber; a pumpkin has non-woody trailing stems. A plant can therefore be described in more than one way.
Climber · grape vine                       Creeper · pumpkin
A climber and a creeper both have stems that need support or spread along the ground. What observations would you need before deciding which receives more light?
So far you have grouped plants using only the stem. Leaves give us another way to sort the same plants. We can compare these groups with the stem groups.
Lines on a Leaf
Hold a leaf up against the light. You will see thin lines running through it. These lines are **veins**. The pattern the veins make is called **venation**.
Veins contain tissues that transport water and dissolved substances. They carry water into the leaf and sugars made in the leaf to other parts of the plant. They also help support the leaf.

Investigate
**You will need:** fallen leaves of at least four different plants, thin paper, a pencil with soft lead.
**What to do:**
1. Put a leaf on the desk with its back side facing up. The veins stand out more on that side.
2. Place a sheet of thin paper over the leaf.
3. Hold the paper still. Rub the side of the pencil lead flat across it, using light strokes.
4. Check the print against the leaf. If the veins are unclear, adjust the paper or pressure and try again.
5. Do this for every leaf. Write the plant's name next to each print.
Put all your prints side by side.
Group the prints by their vein patterns. How many groups does your sample support? Explain your rule. If all the patterns look alike, compare with another group’s leaves.

A rubbing is a record made by a method. A faint patch may mean the paper moved or the pencil missed it. Check that patch on the actual leaf before describing its veins. Keep an unclear print beside your improved one so you can explain why you changed the record.

Compare the vein pattern separately from the leaf outline. Two leaves can have different outlines yet share a vein pattern. Point to the lines that support your grouping; another group should be able to follow your rule without knowing the plant names.
Two Patterns
Compare your prints with these examples. Two common patterns are shown here; your sample may contain only one.
In **reticulate venation**, veins branch to form a net. A thick middle vein is visible in the hibiscus leaf; finer veins branch and join around it. Mango, neem and peepal also have net-like venation.

In other leaves, many veins run alongside one another. This pattern is called **parallel venation**. In a grass blade they run along the length of the leaf. A banana leaf has a strong middle vein, with many parallel side veins running out towards its edges. Parallel venation does not mean that a leaf has no middle vein.
Hibiscus · reticulate             Banana · parallel             Grass · parallel
These two patterns help you compare many of the leaves around you. Look closely: real leaves sometimes show exceptions.
Predict the venation of wheat or maize from the examples. Then inspect a leaf or a clear photograph. Was your prediction supported? Leaf shape alone is not proof of its vein pattern.
Leaves are only part of the comparison. Next, examine roots.
Under the Ground
Roots hold plants in place and take up water and dissolved minerals. You can observe their growth as seeds germinate.

Investigate
**You will need:** a handful of chana (chickpea) seeds, a handful of wheat seeds, two shallow trays or plates, cotton cloth or cotton wool, water.
**What to do:**
1. Soak both kinds of seed in water overnight.
2. Spread a wet cloth in each tray. Put the chana seeds in one tray. Put the wheat seeds in the other.
3. Keep both trays in the same place. Keep the cloth damp, not flooded, and check it every morning for six days.
4. From day three, inspect the seedlings daily. Record when each germinates and sketch the roots without tearing them.
5. On day six, compare several seedlings of each kind. Keep any that germinated late and observe them for a few more days. Do not pull roots out of the cloth; examine them gently.
Draw what grew from each kind of seed in your notebook. Use the same scale for both drawings.
Could drawings alone tell you which plant is harder to pull out? What would you need to keep alike in a comparison of root anchorage?

Give each seedling a small identifying label and date each sketch. This lets you follow one seedling through time instead of mistaking differences between seedlings for changes in one plant. Place a ruler beside it without disturbing the roots; include a scale in your drawing.

Count age from germination as well as recording the calendar date. If one seed germinated on Monday and another on Thursday, drawings made on Friday show different stages of growth. Compare seedlings of similar age before deciding that a difference belongs to the two kinds of plant.
Two Kinds of Root
Compare several seedlings of each kind. Did they germinate at the same time? Root systems change as seedlings develop, so record the age as well as the shape.

A chana seedling usually develops one main root with smaller side roots. A main root of this kind is a **taproot**. Mustard and radish also develop taproots. The enlarged edible part of a radish includes a swollen taproot that stores food.

As the wheat seedling develops, several thin roots appear. Later, more roots grow from the base of the stem, forming a spreading bunch without one dominant main root. These are called **fibrous roots**. Grass, maize and lemongrass have them.
Chana · taproot                              Wheat · fibrous roots
Both root systems anchor plants and take up water and dissolved minerals. Their branching patterns differ; their jobs overlap.
A taproot can grow deep and reach water below the surface. A deep root system can help a plant through a dry spell, although root depth also depends on the species and the soil.
Many fibrous root systems spread through the upper soil. A dense network helps hold loose soil together and take up water near the surface. Some fibrous roots also reach deep into the ground.
A Pattern Appears
You now know two ways to sort plants. One uses leaves. One uses roots.
Can a record of leaf venation help you predict root type? First collect observations, then test any pattern against another plant.

Investigate
**What to do:**
1. With your teacher or gardener, select five kinds of flowering plants with developed leaves and visible roots. Use spare nursery plants, not plants pulled from the wild.
2. Make a notebook table using the headings in Table 2.4. Examine four kinds first and record their venation and root type. Mark unclear features as uncertain.
3. Look for a connection in these four records. Use it to predict the root type of the fifth kind from its leaf. Record the prediction before examining its roots.
4. Check the roots of the fifth kind. Does this new observation support your proposed pattern? Compare results across the class.
5. Handle the roots gently and replant the plants with your teacher’s help.

Table 2.4: Leaf venation and root type
Plant | Venation | Root prediction (fifth plant) | Root observed
Lemongrass | Parallel |  | Fibrous
What happened with the fifth plant? An unclear root or leaf is a reason to examine it again, not to change the record so it fits.
The Two Go Together
Pool the class records. Count how many support a connection and how many do not. Compare the result with these common patterns in flowering plants.
Many familiar flowering plants with reticulate venation develop taproots; those with parallel venation commonly develop fibrous root systems.
*Sadabahar* has net-like veins and a taproot. Chana has net-like veins and a taproot. Lemongrass has parallel veins and fibrous roots. Wheat has parallel veins and fibrous roots.
These are typical associations, not rules without exceptions. Age, how a plant was propagated, and unusual features can affect what you observe. Keep exceptions in the record.
Could another feature help us recognise these groups? Look inside a seed.

Investigate
**What to do:**
1. Soak a few chana seeds and a few maize seeds in water for two days, until they are soft and swollen.
2. Peel the thin outer coat off a soaked chana. Now try to split the seed with your thumbnail.
3. Try gently to separate a soaked maize grain. Do not use a knife or force it apart. Record what you can see; compare with the labelled section afterwards.
Which seed comes apart neatly into two halves? Which one does not?
What Is Inside a Seed

A soaked chana can separate into two fleshy seed leaves called **cotyledons**. They store food for the young plant. Between them is the rest of the embryo, including a tiny root and shoot. Compare your specimen with the labelled illustration. Trace each label to the part it names, then locate that part in your specimen if it is visible.

In maize, one thin cotyledon lies beside the embryo’s tiny shoot and root. The larger pale region is stored food called the **endosperm**; it is not a second cotyledon. Failure to split the grain is not itself proof of the cotyledon count.
Cotyledon number, leaf venation and root type are associated features. The comparison does not show that cotyledon number causes the other two.

Among flowering plants, those whose seeds have two cotyledons are called **dicotyledons**. We say **dicots** for short.
Plants whose seeds have one cotyledon are called **monocotyledons**, or **monocots**.
Seed anatomy: two chana cotyledons; one maize cotyledon beside the endosperm.
Now put all three findings together.

Comparing flowering plants — typical features
 | Dicots | Monocots
Cotyledons in the seed | Two | One
Leaf venation | Reticulate | Parallel
Roots | Taproot | Fibrous
Examples | Chana, mustard, hibiscus, mango | Wheat, maize, grass, banana
If seed anatomy identifies a plant as a monocot, you can predict that it is likely to have parallel venation and fibrous roots. Check those features before claiming the prediction is correct.

Suppose a leaf pattern is clear but the roots have broken during handling. Record the venation as observed and the root type as uncertain. A prediction belongs in a separate column until you can inspect an intact root system. Otherwise, the table would seem to confirm an idea that you had not actually tested.
2.2.2 Grouping Animals
Animals vary as much as plants do. So the same question comes up. Which feature should we use to group them?
Colour or size may be useful for some questions. To compare movement, we need to record how an animal moves and which body parts it uses.
Use your animal records as a starting point. Add observations from direct watching or a reliable video, and identify which source you used.

Investigate
**What to do:**
1. Choose four animals you can safely watch or observe in a reliable video. Include one that moves in more than one way.
2. For each one, write how it moves and which body part it uses.
3. Use Table 2.5 as a guide for your notebook table.
4. Group your animals using the body parts you observed in use. Allow a record to appear in more than one group if your rule requires it.

Table 2.5: How animals move
Animal | How it moves | Body part used
Ant | Walks | Legs
Goat | Walks and jumps | Legs
Pigeon | Walks and flies | Legs and wings
Housefly | Walks and flies | Legs and wings
Fish | Swims | Fins
Earthworm |  |
A pigeon walks and flies. How would you record it in a grouping by body parts used for movement? Would forcing every animal into only one group lose information? Explain with your records.
What Movement Tells Us
Animals move in many ways. They walk, run, hop, crawl, fly, swim and glide. Some do more than one, like a pigeon.

Sorting them this way shows us something interesting. Animals that are not alike at all may still move in the same way, using similar body parts. A housefly and a pigeon are very different creatures. But both have wings, and both fly. A fish and a dolphin look alike in water, even though a dolphin is not a fish.
That is a clue about something you will meet soon in this chapter. The way an animal is built has a lot to do with *where* it lives.

Movement is not the only way to group animals. We can also group them by what they eat, by where they live, or by what covers the body — scales, feathers, fur, or exposed skin. As with plants, the best grouping depends on the question we are asking.
Know a scientist

**Janaki Ammal (1897–1984)** was one of the first Indian women to work as a professional botanist. She studied sugarcane and worked on making plant varieties better. In 1952 she became Officer on Special Duty at the Botanical Survey of India and helped reorganise its work. In her eighties she joined the fight to save the forest at Silent Valley in Kerala. Her whole life was spent doing the two things this chapter is about — looking closely at plants, and finding order in what she saw.
2.3 Living Things and Their Surroundings
Compare your local records with records from another place. You may find both shared and different kinds. Differences in water, temperature, food and shelter can help explain the comparison.

Investigate
**What to do:**
1. Make one shared class table on the blackboard using Table 2.6.
2. As a class, fill it with plants and animals you have seen, read about, or heard about at home.
3. Now look at each column. Ask: what is that place like? Hot or cold? Wet or dry? Windy? Is water easy to find there?

Table 2.6: Living things in different surroundings
Desert | Mountains | Ocean | Forest | Other region
Camel | Deodar tree | Fish | Tiger |
Compare the warm sandy desert and cold mountain conditions in your class table. Which conditions differ? What else would you need to know before predicting whether an animal could survive in both?
Some living things occur in several surroundings; others have a much narrower range. Compare the conditions in each column. The features of a living thing help explain where it can survive.
Built for the Place
Look at a plant from a hot desert.

Consider a cactus adapted to a hot, dry habitat. Its fleshy stem stores water and its waxy surface reduces water loss. In many cacti, leaves are reduced to spines and the green stem carries out photosynthesis.
Now look at a deodar tree, high in the Himalayas.
On snowy mountain slopes, snow can load branches heavily. The conical form and sloping branches of a deodar can help shed snow. Temperature, soil and water also affect where a tree can grow.
Cactus · hot desert                         Deodar · cold mountain
These features were not chosen by individual plants. They are inherited features found in populations living in particular conditions. Other plants may survive there using different features.

Suppose a cactus from a frost-free desert is moved to a place with freezing winters and persistently wet soil. Which new conditions would you investigate before deciding whether it could survive? The word "mountain" alone is not enough information.
Two Camels, Two Deserts
Compare the two kinds of camel in the illustration. Which visible differences could matter in cold weather?

Camels live in the hot sandy desert of Rajasthan. Camels also live in the cold, high, rocky desert of Ladakh. Both places are deserts. Both are dry, with little food and little shelter. But they are dry in very different ways. And the two camels are not the same.
The Rajasthan camel is tall, with long legs. Its two-toed feet have broad, spreading pads. They spread its weight, so it does not sink into loose sand. It has one hump. Its coat is thin.

The Ladakh camel is shorter and heavier. Its sturdy legs also end in broad, padded, two-toed feet. It has two humps. It grows a thick shaggy coat, especially at the head and neck, for winters that fall far below freezing.
Dromedary · one hump                         Bactrian · two humps

You may have heard that a camel stores water in its hump. That is not true. The hump stores fat. The camel lives off that fat when there is no food. When a camel uses much of this stored fat, its humps can become smaller and less upright.

Camels save water in other ways. They pass very little urine. Their dung is dry enough to burn. They can allow their body temperature to rise during the day, reducing the water needed for cooling. They do sweat when necessary. How long a camel can go without drinking depends on heat, activity and the food available.
Adaptations
The cactus stem, the deodar's sloping branches, the camel's padded feet and hump — all of these are examples of one idea.

Inherited features that help organisms survive and reproduce in their usual environment are called **adaptations**. They develop in populations over generations; an individual does not acquire a needed feature simply by trying.

Adaptations are not always about extreme places, and they are not always easy to spot. A fish has a smooth body that slips through water easily, and fins to steer and push with. A duck has skin joining its toes. That turns each foot into a paddle. A pigeon's toes are not joined by broad webbing. Its separate toes help it grip supports and walk.

Rhododendrons include low shrubs and tall trees in different mountain regions. Their features reflect both inherited differences and growing conditions. Even plants of the same species may grow differently in a windy, exposed place and in a sheltered one. A change in one plant's growth is not the same as an inherited adaptation developing over generations.
Two plants of the same species grow in different places, one windy and one sheltered. If their heights differ, what other factors would you check before attributing the difference to wind?
Duck · webbed foot                            Pigeon · no webbing
Habitat
The place where a living thing lives is called its **habitat**.

A habitat includes the conditions and resources an organism uses. Plants need light, water and minerals; animals need food as well as suitable conditions. A habitat need not be safe at all times, and an animal may use different places to feed or breed.
A habitat can be small: damp soil beneath a fallen log differs from the dry path beside it. Such differences help explain why nearby places can hold different living things.
Habitats can be sorted into two broad kinds.
Living things on land live in **terrestrial** habitats. Forests, deserts, grasslands and mountains are terrestrial habitats. So is the ground under your feet.
Living things in water live in **aquatic** habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.

Some animals use both land and water. Frogs belong to a group called **amphibians**; many amphibians spend part of their lives in each. But using both habitats does not make every animal an amphibian. A crocodile does so too, and it is a reptile.
When a Habitat Is Lost
Ask your parents, your grandparents, or an older neighbour one simple question. Which birds, insects or plants did they see often as children, but rarely see now?
Record what the person remembers and where they lived. Memory is a starting point for a question, not proof of a change in population. Look for dated records or photographs to compare.

Habitat damage can reduce food, shelter or breeding sites. Some organisms may move; others may not be able to reach suitable places. Populations can decline or disappear locally. To investigate a decline, check both changes in habitat and how the observations were made.
Know a scientist

**Salim Ali (1896–1987)** spent many years travelling across India, watching birds. He recorded where they lived, when they arrived, and where they went next. Watching carefully like this, year after year, is how scattered sightings turn into real knowledge. His fieldwork and advocacy helped strengthen bird conservation in India. His books also made it possible for ordinary people to name the birds around them. He is remembered as the Birdman of India.

Habitat loss has threatened animals such as the Bengal tiger and the Great Indian bustard. Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats. The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952; a reintroduction programme began in 2022. Protecting suitable habitat is essential to conservation.

Governments and communities both protect habitats. **Sacred groves** are patches of vegetation protected through local cultural or religious traditions. Rules about cutting, collecting and hunting vary. Some groves preserve old trees and habitat missing from nearby cleared land. Some also have legal protection. Find out how a grove near you is protected.
A sacred grove — a surviving patch of forest
Suppose a class records more kinds of birds in a protected grove than in a nearby clearing. Does that record alone show that protection caused the difference?
Check how the records were made. Were both places watched for the same length of time, at similar times of day? Could differences in area, water or vegetation also matter?
Plan repeated visits using the same method. Decide what to record so another class could check your comparison. A useful conclusion must account for both the evidence and its limits.
Keywords

Adaptation: An inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its usual environment.
Amphibian: An animal belonging to the group that includes frogs and toads; many use water and land during their lives.
Aquatic: Living in water, or describing a habitat in water.
Biodiversity: The variety of living things found in a region.
Climber: A plant that grows upwards using external support.
Cotyledon: A seed leaf that is part of the embryo inside a seed.
Creeper: A plant with stems that trail along the ground.
Dicot: A flowering plant whose seed has two cotyledons.
Endosperm: Food-storing tissue in a seed that nourishes the developing embryo.
Fibrous root system: A spreading bunch of roots without one dominant main root.
Grouping: Arranging things by features they share, using a stated rule.
Habitat: The place where an organism lives, including its conditions and resources.
Herb: A plant with soft, non-woody stems; it need not be small.
Monocot: A flowering plant whose seed has one cotyledon.
Parallel venation: A leaf-vein pattern in which many veins run alongside one another.
Pseudostem: A trunk-like structure formed by overlapping leaf bases, as in banana.
Reticulate venation: A leaf-vein pattern in which veins branch and join to form a network.
Sacred grove: A patch of vegetation protected through local cultural or religious traditions.
Shrub: A woody plant that usually branches near the ground, often with several main stems.
Taproot: The main root of a root system, with smaller roots branching from it.
Terrestrial: Living on land, or describing a habitat on land.
Tree: A woody plant that usually develops a main trunk supporting a crown of branches.
Venation: The pattern of veins in a leaf.
Summary
• The variety of living things found in a region is called its biodiversity. Even an ordinary place has much more of it than a quick look suggests.
• Living things in a place depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs.
• Grouping means arranging things by the features they share. Different rules answer different questions; each must be applied consistently.
• Woody stems and branching help distinguish trees and shrubs from non-woody herbs. Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, which can overlap with these descriptions.
• The pattern of veins in a leaf is called venation. Two common patterns are reticulate and parallel.
• Two common root systems are taproot and fibrous root systems. A taproot has one main root. Fibrous roots form a spreading bunch.
• Among flowering plants, dicots have two cotyledons and monocots have one.

• These three features go together. Dicots generally have reticulate venation and a taproot. Monocots generally have parallel venation and fibrous roots. These associations support predictions that must be checked.
• Animals can be grouped by how they move and which body parts they use. They can also be grouped in many other ways.
• Adaptations are inherited features that help organisms survive and reproduce. They develop in populations over generations, not because an individual tries to change.
• The place where a living thing lives is its habitat. Habitats are terrestrial or aquatic. Many amphibians use both land and water, but not all animals that do so are amphibians.
• Damage to habitats causes loss of biodiversity. This is why habitats are protected — by governments, and by communities.

Learning Further

• Walk around your school with your teacher or the gardener. Label the plants with their local names. Make a list in your notebook. For each plant, record whether its stems are woody and how it grows: upright, climbing or trailing. Use herb, shrub or tree where the evidence supports it; more than one description can apply.

• Over one term, build a **class biodiversity register**. Revisit the same places for the same length of time. Record dates, weather and how you searched. Compare records, but treat a missing sighting as "not recorded", not proof of disappearance. Plan another check before concluding that a kind has gone.

• Interview an older person about local plants and animals. Ask where and when they saw them. Compare one recollection with a dated photograph, written record or another account. Identify what remains uncertain.
• Find out if there is a sacred grove, a protected forest or a bird sanctuary near your district. Who protects it? What is it being protected from?

• Read about one Indian scientist working on biodiversity today. Write a short report. You could start with Divya Mudappa, Vidya Athreya, Uma Ramakrishnan, Nandini Velho, Ghazala Shahabuddin, Usha Lachungpa or Divya Karnad.

• Grow chana and wheat again. For each kind, use equal numbers of seeds from the same batch in two trays: one in light and one in darkness. Keep water, tray material and temperature as similar as possible. For seven days, record the number germinating, shoot length and leaf colour at the same time each day. Predict first; compare each seed kind’s light and dark trays separately. Briefly inspect the dark trays and return them to darkness.
